issues.legal_issue: For a major-mineral lease, the Central Government must form the required opinion after consulting the State Government, and the State Government must implement a resulting request to terminate the lease.
material_facts: The leases included leases for silica sand, a major mineral.
The State claimed that consultation had occurred and that the governments had decided to transfer mining operations to a public-sector company.
The Court held that, for major minerals, the Central Government considers the matter after consulting the State Government and may request the State Government to terminate a lease.
issues.conclusion: For a major-mineral lease, the Central Government makes the relevant decision after consultation, and the State Government is bound to implement a request to terminate the lease.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4A(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 assigns the decision and request to the Central Government, following consultation with the State Government; the State Government must act on that request, as indicated by the word “shall.”

rule.if: challenge_to_premature_lease_termination and lease_covers_major_mineral and central_government_consults_state_government and central_government_forms_required_opinion and central_government_requests_termination

predicates.challenge_to_premature_lease_termination: A party challenges a decision to end a mining lease before its scheduled expiry.
predicates.lease_covers_major_mineral: The mining lease concerns a major mineral.
predicates.central_government_consults_state_govern: The Central Government consults the State Government about the proposed lease termination.
predicates.central_government_forms_required_opinio: The Central Government forms an opinion that the proposed termination is expedient for mineral regulation and development.
predicates.central_government_requests_termination: The Central Government requests the State Government to terminate the lease.
predicates.state_government_must_implement_central_: The State Government is required to implement the Central Government’s request to terminate the lease.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns early termination of a major-mineral lease, and the Central Government consults the State Government, forms the required opinion, and requests termination, the State Government must implement that request.

issues.legal_issue: Premature termination of a mining lease cannot be justified merely because a government company is ready to undertake the mining operations; the decision must be based on whether termination of the particular lease would advance mineral regulation and development.
material_facts: The State relied on the public-sector company’s having equipped itself to undertake mining operations.
The Court held that the decision must consider the circumstances of the particular lease and relevant considerations bearing on mineral regulation and development.
The State had not decided to terminate all mining leases, and private leases were also contemplated.
issues.conclusion: Readiness of a government company to undertake mining operations is not, by itself, a sufficient reason to terminate an existing lease prematurely.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4A requires a case-specific assessment of whether premature termination would advance the interest of regulation of mines and mineral development. Section 4A does not direct termination merely because a government company or corporation is ready to undertake the work.

predicates.challenge_to_premature_lease_termination: A party challenges a decision to end a mining lease before its scheduled expiry.
predicates.government_company_is_ready_to_mine: A government company is equipped or ready to undertake the mining operations.
predicates.termination_is_not_supported_by_a_case_s: The decision-maker has not assessed whether ending the particular lease would advance mineral regulation and development.
predicates.company_readiness_alone_does_not_justify: A government company’s readiness, without a case-specific development assessment, is insufficient to justify premature termination.

issues.definition: If early termination is challenged and a government company is ready to mine, but the decision lacks a case-specific assessment of development interests, that readiness alone does not justify early termination.

issues.legal_issue: A lessee affected by an executive decision to terminate a mining lease prematurely must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the final decision.
material_facts: The leases were terminated prematurely by executive action.
The lessees were affected by the termination.
The lessees received no prior notice and no opportunity to present their cases.
The Court found no indication that the governing provision excluded the affected lessees’ right to be heard.
issues.conclusion: A final decision to terminate a lease prematurely can be made only after notice to the lessee and an opportunity for the lessee to present its case.
issues.legal_principle: The principles of natural justice apply where the exercise of power has civil consequences unless their application is specifically excluded. The Court relied on Baldev Singh v. State of Himachal Pradesh, [1987] 2 SCC 510. It distinguished the legislative activity considered in Union of India v. Cynamide India Ltd., AIR 1987 SC 1802, and discussed D.C. Saxena v. State of Haryana, AIR 1987 SC 1463, and State of Tamil Nadu v. Hind Stone, [1981] 2 SCR 742.

rule.if: challenge_to_premature_lease_termination and executive_authority_proposes_to_end_lease_early and lessee_will_face_civil_consequences and governing_law_does_not_exclude_a_hearing

predicates.challenge_to_premature_lease_termination: A party challenges a decision to end a mining lease before its scheduled expiry.
predicates.executive_authority_proposes_to_end_leas: An executive authority proposes to terminate a mining lease before its scheduled expiry.
predicates.lessee_will_face_civil_consequences: The proposed termination will adversely affect the lessee’s rights or interests.
predicates.governing_law_does_not_exclude_a_hearing: The governing law does not expressly exclude the affected lessee’s right to be heard.
predicates.lessee_must_receive_prior_notice_and_opp: The affected lessee must receive notice and an opportunity to present its case before the final termination decision.

issues.definition: When early termination is challenged, an executive authority proposes it, the lessee will face civil consequences, and the governing law does not exclude a hearing, the lessee must first receive notice and an opportunity to be heard.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory framework permits premature termination of leases for minor minerals in appropriate cases.
material_facts: Some of the leases concerned ordinary sand, which is a minor mineral.
The lessees argued that a separate provision excluded the application of Section 4A to minor minerals.
Their counsel did not press that argument before the Court.
issues.conclusion: Leases for minor minerals may also be prematurely terminated in appropriate cases under the statutory framework.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4A(2) makes a provision for minor minerals, distinct from Section 4A(1), which concerns major minerals. Relying on State of Tamil Nadu v. Hind Stone, [1981] 2 SCR 742, the Court held that minor-mineral leases are not altogether excluded from Section 4A by Section 14.

predicates.challenge_to_premature_lease_termination: A party challenges a decision to end a mining lease before its scheduled expiry.
predicates.lease_is_for_a_minor_mineral: The mining lease concerns a minor mineral.
predicates.minor_mineral_lease_may_be_terminated_ea: A lease for a minor mineral may be terminated before expiry when the circumstances and required statutory process make the termination appropriate.

issues.definition: When a challenged early termination concerns a minor-mineral lease, that kind of lease may be terminated early in an appropriate case.

issues.legal_issue: A premature lease termination is unsustainable where the required intergovernmental consultation is ineffective, the Central Government does not form the required opinion, and the affected lessee is not heard.
material_facts: The proposal to terminate the particular leases arose after the public-sector company reported that it was ready to take over mining operations.
The Central Government sought specific information relevant to the proposed terminations, but the State Government did not provide it and instead said the information was irrelevant.
The Central Government later agreed to the proposal while advising that the statutory requirements be complied with.
The affected lessees were not given an opportunity to present their cases.
The Court found no effective consultation and no opinion formed by the Central Government as required.
issues.conclusion: The terminations could not stand; the lessees were entitled to succeed, and the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4A requires effective consultation and formation of the relevant governmental opinion, as well as consideration of the circumstances of the particular lease. Natural justice also requires the affected lessee to be heard before premature termination.

predicates.challenge_to_premature_lease_termination: A party challenges a decision to end a mining lease before its scheduled expiry.
predicates.intergovernmental_consultation_is_ineffe: The governments do not meaningfully exchange and consider information relevant to the proposed termination of the particular lease.
predicates.central_government_does_not_form_require: The Central Government does not form the opinion required to support the proposed termination.
predicates.lessee_is_not_given_a_hearing: The affected lessee receives no opportunity to present its case before the termination decision.

issues.definition: If a challenged early termination follows ineffective intergovernmental consultation, no required opinion by the Central Government, and no hearing for the lessee, the termination cannot stand.
